title: Sample Job Applicant Rejection Letters: 6 Templates for Every Hiring Stage
summary: Enhance your candidate rejection letters with professional, personalized, and honest templates.
body_markdown:
A rejection letter may be the final message a candidate receives from an employer, and some applicants


[receive no response](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/flagships/all-things-work/recruiters-guide-turning-candidates-down-right-way) at all. The 2025


[Fountain Frontline Report](https://ebook.fountain.com/frontline-report-2025) found that 52% of frontline workers name


[candidate ghosting](https://www.fountain.com/posts/3-ways-to-prevent-candidate-ghosting) or a lack of updates as a top frustration. Closing the loop protects your employer brand at little cost and is a practical step any hiring team can take.


Across the


[full frontline funnel](https://www.fountain.com/frontline-hiring) , use automation for application-stage declines and personal outreach after screens, interviews, assessments, or rescinded offers.


## What is a job applicant rejection letter?


A job applicant rejection letter is a written notice telling a candidate they were not selected for a role, stating the decision clearly and giving a brief, job-related reason. Most rejection letters go out as email, and an email rejection isn’t the same thing as the automated ATS notification that fires on a status change.


That notification is fine for candidates who only applied. Once a candidate has invested time in a screen, interview, or assessment,


[more personalized communication](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/flagships/all-things-work/recruiters-guide-turning-candidates-down-right-way) is appropriate.


Tone and detail shift with the stage. A pre-screen rejection can be brief. A finalist rejection should run longer, name specific strengths, and often pair with a phone call. Late-stage candidates warrant personalized


[phone or video communication](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-to-rediscover-and-re-engage-top-candidates) , and that kind of personal delivery supports positive candidate ratings.


## What every rejection letter should include


Every rejection needs an


[unambiguous decision statement](https://recruiters.theguardian.com/advice/candidate-rejection-email-templates) , a brief job-related rationale, and a respectful close that


[thanks the candidate](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-handle-candidate-rejection-matters) for their time. A


[legally conservative baseline](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-reject-job-candidate-defines-recruitment-strategy) is “Thank you for applying, but we have decided to pursue other applicants,” and ending on a high note is nonnegotiable.


Every stage, including the automated application-review note, should come from a


[named sender](https://recruiters.theguardian.com/advice/candidate-rejection-email-templates) on your team rather than a no-reply address.


Keep these four things out of every rejection letter:


- **References to protected characteristics:** Age, race, religion, sex, disability, pregnancy, or national origin have no place in a rejection, directly or through coded language. These are among the


[federally protected characteristics](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/small-business/3-who-protected-employment-discrimination) that cannot lawfully drive a hiring decision.


- **Comparisons to other candidates:** Statements about who was “more qualified”


[can invite a legal challenge](https://www.findlaw.com/legalblogs/small-business/5-legal-tips-for-rejection-letters-emails) ; keep the rejection focused on the role and the decision rather than on who else applied.


- **False encouragement:** “We’ll keep your resume on file” belongs in a letter only if it’s true. Hollow future promises erode trust faster than the rejection itself.


- **Excessive apology or detail:** Over-explaining the decision invites debate and can hand a rejected candidate material for a complaint.


Brief, job-related explanations reduce opportunities for debate later.


## When to send a rejection letter


The loop should close as soon as the decision is final, and communication should become more personal the deeper the candidate got. Employers should notify candidates quickly, while application-only candidates can receive automation and interviewed candidates receive personal outreach.


**Stage** **Recommended cadence** **Method**


Application review


Within


[3 to 5 days](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/candidate-experience-talent-board-research-candes) Automated email


Phone or video screen


Promptly after the decision is final


Personal email from the recruiter


First interview


Promptly after the decision is final


Personal email, or a call if the interview was in person


Final interview


As soon as the decision is final


Phone call, then a follow-up email


Skills assessment


Promptly after the decision is final


Personal email acknowledging the work


Rescinded offer or canceled role


As soon as the decision is final


Phone first, then written confirmation


An instant rejection can make an automated decline feel abrupt. Set a short hold on auto-decline notices so they do not send the instant a recruiter logs the decision. Teams should send rejection communication promptly while keeping the message polite and considered.

## 6 Rejection letter templates for every hiring stage


Each template below is ready to adapt. The optional feedback line belongs in the message only when the feedback is specific and job-related.


### 1. After application review (pre-screen)


**Subject:** Update on your application


Hi there,


After reviewing your application, we will not be advancing it to the next stage. We appreciate your interest in this opportunity with our company.


Thank you for considering our company. If another suitable opening becomes available, we hope you’ll consider applying again. Best wishes with your search.


The recruiting team


### 2. After a phone or video screen


**Subject:** Update on the role with our company


Hi there,


We’ve completed our review and will not be moving your application to the next stage. It was a pleasure speaking with you about the position and hearing more about your experience.


The role’s immediate requirements call for experience that differs from the background discussed during our conversation.


*Optional feedback line:* Hands-on experience with the specific system or equipment used in this role was required for this opening and became the deciding factor.


Thank you for the conversation, and best wishes in your search.


The recruiter


### 3. After a first interview


**Subject:** Your interview with our company


Hi there,


We have now completed this stage and won’t be advancing your application. We appreciate the time you spent interviewing for the position. In particular, we valued the relevant experience you discussed during the interview.


We would still be glad to hear from you if a future opening aligns more closely with your experience.


*Optional feedback line:* For this role, we placed particular weight on experience in a required job-related skill.


Thank you again for your interest in our company.


The recruiter


### 4. After a final interview


Finalists deserve


[timely, personal communication](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-to-rediscover-and-re-engage-top-candidates) , ideally through a phone call before this email lands. They have invested the most in the process.


**Subject:** Following up on our conversation


Hi there,


I appreciate everything you contributed throughout the selection process for the role. As I shared during our call, we have chosen another candidate for this opening.


The decision was difficult. Your experience managing peak-season teams made a strong impression on everyone you met. We would welcome the chance to stay connected about relevant future roles, and I can arrange a feedback call if that would help.


The recruiter


### 5. After a skills assessment


**Subject:** Thank you for completing the assessment


Hi there,


After evaluating the submissions, we have decided not to advance your application. Thank you for completing the assessment or work sample for the opening. We recognize the work involved and especially appreciated the thought you put into your submission.


*Optional feedback line:* Your submission addressed the core task, but one required assessment criterion needed more detail.


We appreciate your interest and hope you’ll consider another suitable role with us in the future.


The recruiter


### 6. After an offer is rescinded or the role is canceled


Legal counsel reviews this letter before it goes out, and the recruiter delivers the news by phone first. Rescissions should be


[communicated verbally first](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/beware-rescinding-job-offers-can-prompt-legal-consequences) , followed by written confirmation (see the legal section below).


**Subject:** Important update regarding your offer


Dear candidate,


This message confirms that our company is withdrawing the offer previously issued for the position. Because of position elimination or organizational restructuring, the company is canceling the role.


This change results from business circumstances and does not reflect your qualifications or the confidence we had in your candidacy. We will contact you about any applicable reimbursement of documented expenses, alternative open roles, or plans to keep your application on file. Please reply to this message if you would like to discuss the decision or next steps.


The hiring team


## How to give feedback (and when not to)


Feedback should be specific, concise, and job-related, and omitted when it cannot meet those standards. This section and the legal guardrails that follow are general information, not legal advice; confirm any specific situation with qualified employment counsel.


Constructive feedback keeps rejected candidates open to


[future opportunities](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/feedback-to-candidates-will-improve-hiring-process) and more likely to share a positive experience.


Feedback hurts when it drifts into personality or speculation. It hurts more when a candidate can read a coded reference to age, health, or family status into the wording. Detailed reasons can backfire in a dispute when a candidate debates the decision or uses the wording in an employment complaint.


At application review you can hold the line at no individualized feedback at all. After a screen or interview, one specific job-related observation is enough, and finalists get fuller feedback, ideally by phone. For requests that arrive after the letter, a practical policy is to answer candidates who ask and keep the response concise.


Pre-approved feedback templates keep hiring managers from improvising language under pressure.


## Legal guardrails: what to never put in writing


As a rule, keep protected characteristics and any comparison to the person hired out of the letter entirely. Federal law shapes what a rejection can say. Title VII, the ADEA, the ADA, and GINA prohibit hiring decisions based on race, color, religion, sex (including pregnancy, sexual orientation, and transgender status), national origin, age 40 or older, disability, and genetic information.


Those


[EEOC protections](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/small-business/3-who-protected-employment-discrimination) apply by statute regardless of what any letter says, so the checklist here is about not creating written evidence that contradicts a lawful decision. Employers should also avoid subjective labels such as “overqualified” and rely instead on objective, job-related criteria, since the ADEA prohibits


[age-based hiring discrimination](https://www.eeoc.gov/fact-sheet/facts-about-age-discrimination) .


Keep the letter brief, but document the decision internally. Record the job-related reason when the decision is made and apply the same criteria to every applicant; later changes to the explanation can be read as


[pretext](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/enforcement-guidance-retaliation-and-related-issues) .


A


[federal retention rule](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1602.14) requires covered hiring records to be kept for at least 1 year, and longer once a charge is filed. Rescinded offers carry their own exposure, including


[promissory estoppel claims](https://www.naceweb.org/career-development/organizational-structure/advisory-opinion-rescinded-and-deferred-employment-offers) when a candidate quit a job or relocated in reliance on the offer, which is why counsel reviews that letter before it goes out.


Employment counsel should review your standard rejection language before it rolls out across locations.


## Rejecting at high volume without ghosting anyone


Stage-matched templates triggered by pipeline transitions give every candidate who exits the funnel the message that fits how far they got, automated for pre-screen exits and personal beyond that. When a team closes out thousands of applicants a week, the question is whether the system can be both fast and human.


The principle is that


[automation fits the early stages](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/candidate-experience-audits-core-to-recruiting) , while candidates receive more personalized care as they progress. Merge-tag personalization needs fallback defaults, so a missing data field produces “Hi Candidate” instead of a broken tag that exposes the automation. Teams can place pre-screen exits on a short delay, and anyone past a phone screen routes to a recruiter before anything goes out.


Manual follow-up is the first thing volume breaks: a recruiter who waits until Friday to email 400 declined applicants may reach only a fraction, and the rest hear nothing.


[Automation covers the volume](https://www.fountain.com/posts/automation-doesnt-replace-recruiters-it-makes-them-better) no one can work by hand, while recruiters keep judgment over every candidate who invested real time, reviewing messages for anyone who completed a screen, interview, or assessment.


With Fountain,


[Fetch](https://www.fountain.com/customer/fetch) (a last-mile delivery platform handling 10,000 applicants a month with three recruiters) saw candidate engagement climb from 0.5 to 5.5 messages per application (with Fountain AI). The lift came from automation, not from recruiters sending each message by hand.


## What a good rejection letter protects: your employer brand


For a high-volume employer, the rejection experience is a major part of the


[employer brand](https://www.fountain.com/posts/employer-branding) . Respectful exits keep candidates warm for the next requisition, encourage them to reapply, and support positive word of mouth. Some reapply when their circumstances change. Ghosted candidates do the opposite, and in retail and quick-service restaurants (QSRs), some are also your customers.


For a frontline operation, the rejection letter helps keep candidates in the talent pool, and it belongs in any high-volume hiring plan. Near-miss candidates create a ready path to a fast fill for later openings, but only if the last message they received made reapplying feel worth it.

## Frequently asked questions about job applicant rejection letters


### Do I have to send a rejection letter?


Send a rejection letter to close the loop with each candidate. Ask qualified counsel whether any separate legal notice is required based on the circumstances and jurisdiction. Closing the loop is still a sound practice.


### Can a rejected candidate take legal action?


Yes. Applicants can file discrimination charges with the EEOC, generally within


[180 calendar days](https://www.eeoc.gov/youth/time-limits-filing-complaint) of the decision, extended to 300 days in some jurisdictions. Consistent, contemporaneous records help show that objective, job-related criteria were established before review and applied consistently.


### How do you reject hundreds of applicants a week without ghosting anyone?


Stage-triggered automation with human oversight. Pre-screen exits get an automated, personalized email on a short delay, and candidates who spoke with a recruiter or completed an assessment route to a person for a message or a call. Every exit from the funnel produces a message, and recruiters spend their time where the candidate’s investment earned it.
